q: Rate is a measure of how fast or how slow the ____ is.
e: Reaction rate quantifies the speed at which reactants are converted into products.

q: To describe the quantitative measurement of a reaction rate, it is necessary to specify how fast the reactants are used up or the ____ are formed.
e: Rates can be measured by tracking the disappearance of reactants or the appearance of products over time.

q: The rate of reaction means measuring the change in the amount of a product produced or a reactant used up in the ____ taken for that change.
e: Time is the fundamental variable in the denominator of any reaction rate expression.

q: The reaction rate is usually expressed as the change in the amount of a reactant used up or the product formed in a unit of ____.
e: Rate is always expressed as a change in quantity per unit time.

q: If the substance is a gas, the amount consumed or formed is expressed in pressure units or as measured in ____.
e: Gaseous reactants or products can be monitored by measuring changes in their volume or pressure.

q: ____ units are used if the reactant or product is in solution.
e: For reactions in solution, molar concentration is the standard unit for measuring the amount of substance.

q: Generally, in chemical reactions, the rate of a reaction in solution is measured in terms of a decrease in the concentration of the reactant or an increase in the concentration of the product per unit time at a constant ____.
e: Temperature must be kept constant when measuring reaction rates because it significantly affects the rate.

q: In the rate equation, the delta ($\Delta$) means ____.
e: The delta symbol represents the difference between final and initial values of a quantity.

q: In the rate equation, the square bracket [] represents molar ____.
e: Square brackets are the standard chemical notation for expressing molar concentration (mol/dm³).

q: The minus (-) sign means a ____ in the concentration of the reactant.
e: Reactants are consumed during a reaction, so their change in concentration is negative, requiring a minus sign to make the rate positive.

q: The plus (+) sign means an ____ in the concentration of the product.
e: Products are formed during a reaction, resulting in a positive change in their concentration.

q: Rate is expressed as a ____ quantity.
e: By convention, reaction rates are always reported as positive values regardless of whether tracking reactants or products.

q: In a general chemical reaction, a, b, c, and d are the stoichiometric ____ of the reactants and products in the balanced chemical equation.
e: Stoichiometric coefficients are necessary to relate the rates of consumption and formation of different species in a reaction.

q: The rate constant, k, explains the relationship between the molar concentration of the reactants and the ____ of a chemical reaction.
e: The rate constant k is the proportionality factor in the rate law equation linking concentration to reaction rate.

q: The mole ratios from the balanced chemical equation can be used to determine the rates of change in ____ of products and reactants.
e: Stoichiometry allows the conversion of the rate of one substance to the rate of another in the same reaction.

q: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid giving off ____ gas.
e: The reaction between a reactive metal and an acid typically produces a salt and hydrogen gas.

q: The volume of hydrogen gas released in the process of reaction at time intervals can be ____.
e: Gas syringes or water displacement methods are used to measure the volume of gas evolved over time.

q: The time measurement is expressed in whatever units fit the reaction (seconds, minutes, hours, days, months or ____).
e: The time unit chosen depends on the speed of the reaction, ranging from seconds for fast reactions to years for very slow ones.

q: ____ theory explains how chemical reactions occur.
e: Collision theory provides the fundamental framework for understanding reaction kinetics at the molecular level.

q: Collision theory is based on the kinetic molecular theory of ____.
e: The principles of gas particle motion are applied to reacting molecules in collision theory.

q: Reactant particles moving in random directions possess ____ energy.
e: The motion of particles gives them kinetic energy, which is necessary for collisions to occur.

q: Not all collisions between reactant particles result in the formation of reaction ____.
e: Only a fraction of collisions have the correct orientation and sufficient energy to yield products.

q: For a reaction to occur, colliding particles must possess a certain minimum energy known as an ____ energy.
e: Activation energy is the energy threshold that must be overcome for a successful reaction to take place.

q: During a collision, the spatial ____ of the reactant molecules is important to determine whether or not a reaction occurs.
e: Molecules must collide with the correct geometric alignment for bonds to break and form properly.

q: If the colliding particles have the incorrect orientation, they will ____ off each other.
e: Unsuccessful collisions due to poor orientation result in the particles simply bouncing apart without reacting.

q: The unsuccessful collisions with insufficient energy do not produce a ____.
e: Collisions lacking the activation energy cannot break the necessary bonds to initiate a chemical change.

q: When the particles collide with the correct orientation, they must have enough energy for a successful collision (____ collision) to produce a reaction.
e: An effective collision is one that possesses both the correct orientation and sufficient activation energy.

q: The rate of reaction depends on the rate of successful collisions between reactant ____.
e: The overall macroscopic reaction rate is directly proportional to the frequency of effective microscopic collisions.

q: Reacting particles must collide with sufficient energy to form the activated ____.
e: The activated complex is the high-energy, transitional arrangement of atoms formed at the peak of the collision.

q: The activated complex is a temporary species formed by the reactant particles as a result of the collision before they form the ____.
e: This unstable intermediate state exists momentarily before collapsing into either products or reverting to reactants.

q: The more successful collisions there are, the more the activated complex leads to the rate of a reaction being ____.
e: A higher frequency of effective collisions directly translates to a faster macroscopic reaction rate.

q: In the molecular view of the matter, it is postulated that chemical reactions depend on the collisions between the reacting particles - atoms, molecules or ____.
e: Collision theory applies to all types of reacting species, including neutral molecules and charged ions.

q: Reacting particles (atoms, molecules, or ions) must collide in the correct orientation with sufficient energy to overcome the energy ____ to react.
e: The activation energy acts as an energy barrier that prevents all collisions from resulting in a reaction.

q: According to the collision theory, a reaction will speed up if the frequency of collision ____.
e: More frequent collisions increase the probability of effective collisions occurring per unit time.

q: According to the collision theory, a reaction will speed up if the proportion of particles with energy that is greater than the activation energy ____.
e: A larger fraction of energetic particles means a higher percentage of collisions will be successful.

q: Collision theory can be used to explain the main factors such as concentration, temperature, pressure, and particle ____, affecting the rate of chemical reactions.
e: These macroscopic variables alter either the collision frequency or the collision energy at the molecular level.

q: The activation energy ($E_a$) is the minimum energy that reactant particles must possess for a successful collision to take place in a ____.
e: $E_a$ is the specific energy threshold required to initiate the bond-breaking and bond-forming processes.

q: During the progress of a reaction, an unstable intermediate which is known as an activated complex, having required minimum energy, is formed before producing a ____.
e: The activated complex represents the transition state between reactants and final products.

q: In order to get the product, the reactants must pass through a short-lived, high-energy ____ state.
e: The transition state is the peak of the energy profile diagram where old bonds are breaking and new ones are forming.

q: The minimum energy that needs to be reached in this state is equal to the activation energy ($E_a$) for that ____.
e: Every specific chemical reaction has its own unique activation energy value.

q: Hence, the activation energy represents an energy ____ for the reaction, and it has a different value in different reactions.
e: This barrier prevents low-energy collisions from causing unwanted chemical changes.

q: In an exothermic reaction, since the final product has ____ energy than that of the reactants, energy is released.
e: Exothermic reactions release heat because the products are at a lower, more stable energy level than the reactants.

q: Some energy is released when the activated complex leads to the formation of the ____.
e: As the transition state collapses into stable products, the excess energy is released to the surroundings.

q: When there is sufficient energy to overcome the energy barrier, the formation of the product is ____.
e: Surmounting the activation energy barrier allows the reaction pathway to proceed towards products.

q: If the energy is not enough, it cannot overcome the energy barrier and the decomposition of the product, that is, back to reactants will ____.
e: Without enough energy to cross the barrier, the particles simply separate back into their original reactant forms.

q: A high $E_a$ means that relatively few collisions have the required energy to produce the activated complex, and hence, the reaction rate is ____.
e: Reactions with large activation energies proceed slowly because only a tiny fraction of collisions are energetic enough.

q: With a low $E_a$, more collisions have sufficient energy to react, and the reaction rate is ____.
e: Reactions with small activation energies proceed rapidly because a large proportion of collisions are successful.

q: A hydrogen molecule and an iodine molecule collide to form an unstable intermediate $[H_2I_2]$ which exists for a short time and then breaks up to form two molecules of hydrogen ____.
e: The reaction between hydrogen and iodine gases yields hydrogen iodide via a transient activated complex.

q: For many reactions involving liquids or gases, increasing the concentrations of the reactants ____ the rate of reactions.
e: Higher concentration means more particles in a given volume, leading to more frequent collisions.

q: The effect of concentration on the rate of reaction can be explained by the ____ theory.
e: Collision theory links macroscopic concentration changes to microscopic collision frequencies.

q: If more molecules or ions of the reactants are in the reaction area, then there is a greater chance of more effective collisions per unit ____.
e: Crowding more particles into the same space increases the collision rate per second.

q: In reactions involving solids, a reaction occurs at the boundary ____ between reactants.
e: Only the particles exposed on the exterior of a solid can collide with the other reactant.

q: The rate of a reaction involving a solid reactant is increased by increasing the surface ____ of the solid.
e: Crushing a solid exposes more interior particles to the surrounding reactant molecules.

q: The smaller the particle size, the larger the surface ____ will be.
e: Dividing a solid into smaller pieces exponentially increases its total exposed surface area.

q: Reducing the size of particles increases the surface area, increases the number of collisions per second, increases the number of effective collisions, and thus increases the rate of ____.
e: Greater surface area directly translates to a faster overall macroscopic reaction rate.

q: Changing the pressure does not affect the rate of reaction that only involves solids or ____.
e: Solids and liquids are virtually incompressible, so pressure changes do not alter their concentrations.

q: Pressure affects the rate of a reaction involving ____.
e: Gases are compressible, so increasing pressure forces gas molecules closer together, increasing concentration.

q: Increasing the pressure increases the ____ of the reaction.
e: Higher gas pressure leads to more frequent collisions and a faster reaction rate.

q: The pressure is inversely proportional to the volume of a gas at a constant ____.
e: According to Boyle's Law, compressing a gas (decreasing volume) increases its pressure if temperature is constant.

q: At low pressure, the volume becomes larger, the number of collisions of gaseous molecules is smaller, and thus, the rate of reaction is ____.
e: Expanded gases have particles further apart, reducing collision frequency and slowing the reaction.

q: At high pressure, the volume becomes smaller, the number of collisions is greater, and thus, the rate of reaction is ____.
e: Compressed gases have particles crowded together, increasing collision frequency and speeding up the reaction.

q: Most chemical reactions react faster at a high temperature than at a low ____.
e: Temperature is one of the most significant factors influencing the speed of a chemical reaction.

q: The kinetic energy of a gas is directly proportional to the ____.
e: Heating a system increases the average kinetic energy and speed of its particles.

q: Increasing the temperature also increases the kinetic energy, which means that the molecules move faster and collide more frequently with sufficient activation energy for the reaction to ____.
e: Higher temperatures ensure that a larger fraction of collisions possess the necessary energy to react.

q: Thus, the number of effective collisions per second of the reacting particles increases, and hence, the rate of reaction ____.
e: The dual effect of more frequent collisions and more energetic collisions drastically speeds up the reaction.

q: The effect of temperature on reaction rates can also be explained by using the energy distribution curve also known as the ____ distribution.
e: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution graphically shows the spread of kinetic energies among molecules at a given temperature.

q: In general, the area under the Boltzmann distribution curve represents the number of particles within a certain energy ____.
e: The curve plots the fraction of molecules against their specific kinetic energy values.

q: The shaded area under the curve shows the number of particles with energy greater than the activation ____.
e: Only the molecules in this shaded region have enough energy to successfully react upon collision.

q: When the temperature is increased, the shape of the distribution curve flattens and spreads out, showing that the fraction of molecules with energy greater than $E_a$ is much ____ at the higher temperature.
e: A higher temperature shifts the peak to the right, significantly increasing the proportion of highly energetic molecules.

q: Generally, for a ten degrees rise in temperature, the area under the curve approximately doubles as does the ____ of reactions.
e: This is a common rule of thumb in kinetics: a 10°C increase often doubles the reaction rate.

q: A catalyst is defined as a substance which alters the rate of a chemical reaction but remains chemically ____ at the end of the reaction.
e: Catalysts participate in the reaction mechanism but are regenerated, leaving their overall mass and chemical state unaltered.

q: Most catalysts make chemical reactions go ____.
e: In industrial and biological contexts, catalysts are primarily used to accelerate sluggish reactions.

q: Catalysts that make chemical reactions go faster are known as ____ catalysts.
e: Positive catalysts lower the activation energy, providing a faster pathway for the reaction.

q: Sometimes, a chemical reaction needs to go more slowly or suppress unwanted reactions using a ____ catalyst.
e: Negative catalysts (inhibitors) increase the activation energy or block reaction pathways to slow down degradation.

q: Generally, the catalysts provide an alternative pathway for the reaction with lower activation energy, and thus increasing the reaction ____.
e: By lowering the energy barrier, a catalyst allows more particles to react at the same temperature.

q: Catalysts may be homogeneous, that is, uniformly mixed with the reactants, or heterogeneous, in which case the catalyst and the reactants are in different ____.
e: The physical state of the catalyst relative to the reactants determines whether it is homogeneous or heterogeneous.

q: Homogeneous catalysts most often catalyse the gaseous and aqueous reactions to increase their reaction ____.
e: Being in the same phase allows homogeneous catalysts to interact intimately with all reactant molecules.

q: Most heterogeneous catalysts are solids that catalyse either gaseous or liquid ____.
e: Solid catalysts are widely used in industry because they are easily separated from fluid reaction mixtures.

q: In heterogeneous catalysis, the reactions take place on the surface of the solid catalyst to speed ____.
e: Reactant molecules must adsorb onto the active sites of the solid surface to undergo the catalysed reaction.

q: Catalysts are important for the proper functioning of the biological ____.
e: Life relies heavily on catalysis to sustain the complex metabolic pathways required for survival.

q: Enzymes act as biocatalysts for specific biochemical reactions in living ____.
e: Enzymes are highly specialized protein catalysts that regulate virtually all chemical processes in cells.

q: In general, the reaction rate using enzymes is much faster than inorganic catalysts, often increased by a factor of $10^6$ to ____.
e: Enzymes are extraordinarily efficient, capable of accelerating reactions millions to trillions of times faster than uncatalysed rates.

q: Some chemical reactions obtain the energy they need from ____.
e: Photons provide the necessary activation energy for certain light-sensitive chemical processes.

q: Reactions that are initiated by light are called photochemical ____.
e: These reactions require the absorption of electromagnetic radiation to proceed.

q: The brighter the light, the faster is the ____.
e: Higher light intensity means more photons are available to excite reactant molecules per second.

q: If the intensity of light (visible or ultraviolet) is greater, the more reactant molecules gain the energy to absorb the ____.
e: Absorption of light energy promotes molecules to an excited state, enabling them to react.

q: When molecules absorb the light ($h\nu$), a photochemical reaction takes place, such as photosynthesis in green ____.
e: Photosynthesis is a vital biological photochemical reaction driven by sunlight.

q: Storage of preserved foods at a sub-zero temperature is effective in slowing the rate of bacterial ____.
e: Freezing drastically reduces the kinetic energy of molecules, slowing down the biological and chemical reactions that cause spoilage.

q: When large amounts of flammable powdered substances collect in grain elevators, coal mines and chemical industries, violent explosions can ____.
e: Fine powders have massive surface areas, allowing for extremely rapid oxidation reactions that can lead to explosions.

q: At high altitudes with low temperature and low pressure, it takes a long time to ____ an egg.
e: Lower atmospheric pressure at high altitudes reduces the boiling point of water, slowing down the cooking process.

q: Corrosion inhibitors like imidazoline and quaternary amine prevent $H_2S$ and $CO_2$ ____.
e: These negative catalysts form protective layers on metals to slow down destructive oxidation reactions.

q: Volatile corrosion inhibitors (VCI) such as morpholine or hydrazine prevent corrosion in ____.
e: VCIs vaporize and condense on metal surfaces inside closed systems like boilers to protect them from rust.

q: Wrapping metals in volatile corrosion inhibitor-coated paper is common for short-term protection against moisture and ____.
e: The inhibitors slowly release from the paper to create a protective vapor barrier around the metal.

q: Zinc granule reacts fairly slowly with dilute hydrochloric acid but much faster with the more concentrated hydrochloric acid as a function of ____.
e: Monitoring the volume of gas evolved over time clearly demonstrates the effect of concentration on reaction speed.

q: Aluminium foil reacts moderately with sodium hydroxide solution only when warmed, but powdered aluminium of the same mass reacts rapidly in the ____.
e: The massive increase in surface area of the powder compensates for the lack of thermal energy.

q: Large pieces of wood are difficult to ignite whereas small pieces burn more ____.
e: Smaller pieces of wood have a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio, allowing oxygen to react faster.

q: Food can cook faster in a pressure cooker than in a pot, because trapped steam becomes hotter as the pressure ____.
e: Higher pressure raises the boiling point of water, allowing food to cook at a much higher temperature.

q: The time required to hard-boil an egg in water is much shorter at 100°C than at ____.
e: The higher temperature provides more kinetic energy, vastly accelerating the protein denaturation reactions.

q: Foods are cooled or frozen to slow down the chemical reactions that result in the spoiling of ____.
e: Refrigeration lowers the temperature, decreasing the rate of bacterial and enzymatic degradation.

q: In the manufacturing process of sulphuric acid, nitrogen oxide acts as a catalyst in the oxidation of sulphur ____.
e: Nitrogen oxide acts as a homogeneous catalyst in the Lead Chamber process to convert $SO_2$ to $SO_3$.

q: In the ammonia oxidation process (Ostwald process), Pt - Rh catalyst speeds up the ____.
e: The platinum-rhodium gauze acts as a heterogeneous catalyst to oxidize ammonia into nitric oxide.

q: The most well-known digestive enzymes, ptyalin in saliva and pepsin in gastric juice, catalyse to hasten the breakdown of large molecules, such as starch and protein, into simpler ____.
e: Digestive enzymes hydrolyze complex macromolecules into smaller, absorbable units.

q: The reaction between hydrogen and chlorine is extremely slow in the dark, but it becomes explosive when the reaction mixture is exposed to intense sunlight via a chain ____.
e: Light initiates a free-radical chain reaction that propagates explosively once started.
